clue.text: Club in which Daft Punk record initially broke

indicators.note: the club is the container, and the rest of the wordplay sits inside it

parts.note: a bat is a club used in cricket or baseball

indicators.note: daft means silly or crazy, so the letters of punk go haywire
initially points to the opening letter of the word record

explanation.surface: A clubgoer recalls the moment a Daft Punk track first started playing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daft' looks like part of the band's name but signals the anagram; the R from 'record' joins the shuffled letters, which 'in which' places inside the club.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone broke has no money left, exactly the state of a person declared insolvent.

clue.text: A scribbled note reportedly intended to make amends

indicators.note: something scribbled is dashed off messily, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters of note, taken as written for the anagram

indicators.note: reportedly signals that a word is heard rather than seen

parts.note: intended means meant, which is heard here

explanation.surface: Someone dashes off a quick note of apology to put things right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scribbled' turns NOTE into TONE; 'reportedly' gives MENT, which is said the same as MEANT (intended). 'to make' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Amends are reparation for a wrong, the same idea as making up for a sin or offence.

clue.text: Legitimate knockout finishes off contender before middle of the second round

indicators.note: before here simply links the turned pair to the closing letters taken from contender

parts.note: KO is the standard boxing abbreviation for a knockout

indicators.note: round means turned about, so this short run of letters is read backwards
middle of picks the central letter of the word the
only the finishing pair of the word contender survives, the rest being cut away

explanation.surface: A boxing commentator says a knockout was legitimate, ending the contender's hopes in round two.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' turns HS (middle of 'the' plus S for second) into SH; 'finishes off' leaves ER from 'contender', the turned pair being set before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Kosher literally means fit under Jewish dietary law, and informally means genuine or above board.

clue.text: Still down after removal of control panel?

definitions.meaning: still feeling low, not yet comforted out of one's sadness
read whimsically as un- plus console plus -d: having had one's console taken away

explanation.surface: A technician describes a machine that stays off once its control panel is removed.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is a joke: a console is a control panel, so to 'un-console' something would be to strip it of one.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone still down has not been comforted, which is literally what the word describes.

clue.text: Two notes forming a perfect fourth interval

definitions.text: Two notes forming a perfect fourth
definitions.meaning: in sol-fa, ti up to mi spans a perfect fourth, and the two syllables written together spell the entry
a stretch or gap, as in a period between events

explanation.surface: A music lesson on which two notes make up the interval called a perfect fourth.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading describes the sol-fa notes TI and ME (a variant of mi) side by side; time is also the fourth dimension, which adds to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An interval is a stretch of duration between two events, such as a gap or pause.

clue.text: Host related to member?

definitions.meaning: a host is a great multitude, especially of soldiers
jokingly, like a limb: a member is an arm, and -y makes an adjective

explanation.surface: Is a party host somehow related to one of the club's members?
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading treats the word as arm plus the adjective ending -y; member is an old word for a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A host in the old sense is a large body of fighting men, the same as a military force.

clue.text: Accountant wanting almost everything increased and added up

indicators.note: the word accountant lacks all but its opening letter

parts.note: mounted means rose or increased, as costs mount

explanation.surface: An accountant, short of nearly everything, watches the bills mount and add up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting almost everything' leaves only the A of 'Accountant'; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Amounted to means totalled, the result when figures are summed.

clue.text: See 22
Floppy disc saves into memory when initialised

indicators.note: saves means keeps safe, so the disc holds the other letters inside

parts.note: LP is a long-playing record, a vinyl disc

indicators.note: initialised means reduced to initials, so the words into and memory give their first letters

explanation.surface: An old floppy disk stores files into a computer's memory once formatted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when initialised' gives I and M, which 'saves' puts inside LP. 'Floppy disc' looks like a computer term but 'Floppy' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Floppy and limp both describe something slack that hangs loosely without stiffness.

clue.text: Judgement of one lacking in feeling

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: sentience is the capacity for feeling
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A judge's ruling on someone who seems to lack any feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' removes I (one) from SENTIENCE; 'of' and 'in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentence is a court's judgement, the punishment a judge passes.

clue.text: Sculpt solid representations that are highly regarded

indicators.note: to sculpt is to shape material, so these letters are remodelled

explanation.surface: An instruction to carve solid statues that people admire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sculpt' reshapes the letters of SOLID.
explanation.definitionFit: Idols are images worshipped as gods, and also people or figures much admired.

clue.text: I'm surprised about politician with confident self-assurance

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the exclamation wraps round the politician

parts.note: coo is an exclamation of surprise
MP is a Member of Parliament
sure means confident

explanation.surface: Someone expresses surprise at how coolly assured a politician seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coo!' is a British exclamation of mild surprise; 'about' wraps it round the politician, and 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Composure is calmness and self-possession, a steady assurance under pressure.

clue.text: Author regularly obtaining right support for child

indicators.note: regularly says the insertions come at even spacing, so the golf peg goes in one letter further along
obtaining means getting hold of, so the writer takes in the letter for right

parts.note: to pen is to write, as an author does
a tee is the peg supporting a golf ball

explanation.surface: A writer regularly gets the right backing for a children's book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' explains the spacing: one piece goes after the first letter of the writer word, the other after its second. 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A preteen is a youngster aged about nine to twelve, not yet a teenager.

clue.text: Turn upside down yet remain vertical essentially

indicators.note: essentially means at the core, so the letters sit within the words remain vertical

explanation.surface: A puzzle about turning something over while it still stands upright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'essentially' picks the letters out of 'remaIN VERTical'; 'yet' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To invert something is to put it the other way up, reversing its orientation.

clue.text: How one could refer to man spending time in prison

definitions.text: How one could refer to man

indicators.note: spending means giving up or using up, so a letter is lost

parts.note: stir is slang for prison

explanation.surface: How to describe a man serving a sentence behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spending' takes T (time) out of STIR; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir is the polite form of address for a man, as when speaking to a stranger.

clue.text: Irregular verb relies on recall being identical?

indicators.note: irregular means not following the usual pattern, so these letters are disordered

explanation.surface: A grammar note on an irregular verb whose recalled form looks the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irregular' rearranges VERB RELIES. The definition is a playful description: something that reads the same when called back.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can be turned back and still look the same works both ways round.

clue.text: He regularly contributes to protect poorest protest opponents' project

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the word protect is taken

explanation.surface: A campaigner regularly backs schemes protecting the poorest, and opponents of protests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the odd letters of 'protect'; the joke is that 'poorest', 'protest', 'project' and the even letters of 'opponents' give the same four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of verse is typically referred to as a man in older usage, so he stands for one.

clue.text: Position leads to new technological advances in embryonic life-support system

parts.note: a place is a position

indicators.note: leads are the front runners, so the opening letters of the words new, technological and advances are taken

explanation.surface: A news piece on how a position leads to new tech advances in womb care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads to' gives N, T and A; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The placenta nourishes the developing foetus in the womb, supplying oxygen and food through the cord.

clue.text: Name on naked self-portrait with delicate frame

indicators.note: in an across clue, on places the abbreviation directly after the other piece
naked means stripped bare, so the outer letters are removed

parts.note: a selfie is a self-portrait taken on a phone

explanation.surface: Someone posts their name on a nude selfie showing off a slender figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naked' strips the outer letters of the self-portrait word, and 'on' places the name letter after what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Elfin means small and slight like an elf, so having a delicate build.

clue.text: Cologne newspaper divides country

indicators.note: divides means splits apart, so the newspaper goes into the middle of the country

parts.note: France is a country
rag is slang for a low-quality newspaper

explanation.surface: A German city's newspaper causes division in a neighbouring country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cologne' looks like the German city but is eau de Cologne, a scent.
explanation.definitionFit: Cologne is a light perfume, a pleasant scent worn on the skin.

clue.text: Accepted having central characters destroyed by ring that's "precious"

indicators.note: the middle two letters of the word are knocked out and something else takes their place

parts.note: believed means accepted as true
O looks like a ring

explanation.surface: A Tolkien-ish tale: the precious ring destroys what once was trusted.
explanation.walkthrough: IE, the middle of BELIEVED, is replaced by O. The quoted 'precious' echoes Gollum's ring in The Lord of the Rings.
explanation.definitionFit: Something precious to you is dearly loved, as a cherished person or possession.

clue.text: Balkan woman upset about long trousers

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the reversed word goes round the craving
in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a Serb, a native of Serbia in the Balkans
to long for is to itch for

explanation.surface: A Balkan woman is upset about wanting long trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns the word over, giving BRES. 'long' looks like an adjective for the trousers but is the verb meaning crave.
explanation.definitionFit: Britches is a variant spelling of breeches, an old informal word for trousers.

clue.text: Behind, not having succeeded in final course

indicators.note: not having means lacking, so a letter goes

parts.note: afters is British slang for dessert, the last course of a meal
S is the genealogical abbreviation for succeeded

explanation.surface: A student lags behind after failing the final course.
explanation.walkthrough: AFTERS is British for pudding or dessert; 'not having' drops S (succeeded). 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: After and behind both mean following later in place or time.

clue.text: After leaving hospital, pursue patient

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so a letter goes out

parts.note: to chase is to pursue
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: After being discharged, a doctor follows up a patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After leaving' removes H (hospital) from CHASE.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctors speak of a patient as a case, a person under treatment.

clue.text: Profit by Republican in rebellious mood being guest of Tea Party

indicators.note: in means inside, so the party's letter goes into the shuffled word
rebellious means unruly, so the letters of mood break out of order

parts.note: to profit by something is to use it

explanation.surface: A Republican in a rebellious mood benefits from attending a Tea Party rally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rebellious' gives DOMO, and 'in' places R inside it for DORMO. The Tea Party is not American politics but the Mad Hatter's in Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: The sleepy rodent sits at the Mad Hatter's tea table in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

clue.text: Cowboy is clumsy, scratching bottom with end of lasso

indicators.note: scratching means cancelling, and the bottom of a down entry is its last letter

parts.note: gauche means clumsy or awkward

indicators.note: end of takes the final letter of the word lasso

explanation.surface: A clumsy cowboy scratches himself with the end of his lasso.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scratching bottom' cuts the last E from GAUCHE, and 'end of' adds O from 'lasso'. 'is' and 'with' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaucho is a cowboy of the South American pampas, herding cattle on horseback.

clue.text: Dancing feet left without skin and exhausted

indicators.note: without its skin means the outer letters are peeled away, so the middle of the word left remains
dancing feet move about, so the letters of feet shift

explanation.surface: Dancing has left someone's feet raw and worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without skin' leaves EF from 'left', and 'Dancing' turns FEET into FETE.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete means worn out and feeble, having lost one's former vigour.

clue.text: Lower frequency note shields noise

indicators.note: shields means surrounds protectively, so the two letters enclose the din

parts.note: a row is a loud noise

explanation.surface: A sound engineer lowers the frequency of a note to block out noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' looks like a comparative but is the verb meaning scowl (rhymes with 'flower').
explanation.definitionFit: To lower, rhyming with flower, is to scowl or look sullen and threatening.

clue.text: Run out following dispute with flighty creature?

indicators.note: following places the cricket abbreviation after the argument

parts.note: to spar is to argue or dispute
RO is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out

explanation.surface: Someone storms off after an argument with a fickle partner.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a batsman 'run out' is recorded as RO. The definition plays on 'flighty' as able to fly, not fickle.
explanation.definitionFit: A small common bird is literally a creature of flight, so the question mark flags the pun on fickle.

clue.text: Some of the reasons reporter's learned?

indicators.note: a reporter speaks the news, so the word is heard, not read

parts.note: learned means wise

explanation.surface: A journalist asks what reasons the reporter has discovered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'learned' looks like a past tense but is the adjective, pronounced as two syllables.
explanation.definitionFit: As in the whys and wherefores, the plural noun means explanations or causes.

clue.text: Accept not having right order in advance

indicators.note: not having means going without, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: to brook is to tolerate or accept

explanation.surface: A refusal to accept that one has no right to order ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not having' removes R from BROOK.
explanation.definitionFit: To book is to reserve, arranging something such as a table or seat ahead of time.

clue.text: One changing locks in church also turned in grave

indicators.note: in means inside, so the turned letters go within the grave

parts.note: a tomb is a grave

indicators.note: turned means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: too means also

explanation.surface: A locksmith working in a church is turning in his grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' gives OOTHC, which 'in' places inside the grave. 'locks' looks like the door kind but means hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine-toothed comb rearranges hair, and locks are tresses of hair.

clue.text: Knowing may dishearten Nancy or just upset her

parts.note: can and may both express being allowed

indicators.note: dishearten here means removing the heart, so only the outer letters of Nancy stay

explanation.surface: Knowing you might upset Nancy, or simply annoy her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dishearten' leaves NY from 'Nancy'; the clue also offers a second route, since 'upset her' rearranges NANCY to the same letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Canny means shrewd and astute, someone sharp and knowing in judgement.

clue.text: Extra money's not Britain's responsibility

indicators.note: not means without, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: a bonus is extra money, the 's meaning is
B is the abbreviation for Britain

explanation.surface: Extra pay is not something Britain is responsible for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' drops B (Britain) from BONUS.
explanation.definitionFit: An onus is a burden or duty that falls on someone.

clue.text: Faint hum after changing ends at Wimbledon nothing interrupts

indicators.note: interrupts means breaks into, so the tennis score is placed inside
the smell word swaps its first and last letters, which here is the same as reading it backwards

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell, a reek
love is the tennis term for a zero score

explanation.surface: A tennis player faints amid a hum of noise after changing ends at Wimbledon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing ends' swaps the outer letters of the smell word, giving KEER, and 'interrupts' places the tennis zero inside. Hum is British slang for a stink.
explanation.definitionFit: To keel over is to collapse or fall down suddenly, as in a swoon.
